title: Get started — browser & download
combinedTranscript: Learn in your browser first. You do not need to install anything to start Module 1 online. Open Start Here, pick Python, C sharp, or A I, and mark steps done as you go. When you want files on your computer, use GitHub’s Code menu and choose Download ZIP. Find the file in Downloads, then unzip it. Git is optional — beginners can use the ZIP. Open the right folder for your course. Python lives in python-beginner-workbook. C sharp lives in csharp-beginner-workbook. Always start with Module 1 setup. Quick tip: if a download goes missing, check the Help page. You can keep learning online while installers run in the background.

title: Python — download, install, first script
combinedTranscript: Install Python from python.org slash downloads. On Windows, tick Add Python to PATH before you install. On Mac or Linux, use the installer or python 3. Verify it worked. Open a terminal and run python dash dash version, or python 3 dash dash version. You should see a version number. Install a code editor such as Cursor or Visual Studio Code. Add the Python extension, then open your python-beginner-workbook folder. Create hello.py with a print hello message, then run python hello.py. Change the text — that is your first real program. If Windows cannot find Python, reinstall and tick Add to PATH. Use the editor terminal, finish Module 1 exercises, then take the quiz.

title: C# — install .NET and first project
combinedTranscript: Install the dot net S D K from dotnet.microsoft.com slash download. Get the latest S D K, run the installer, then finish. Open a terminal and run dotnet dash dash version. A number like 8 point 0 means you are ready. Install Cursor or Visual Studio Code, add the C sharp Dev Kit extension, and open the csharp-beginner-workbook folder. Create a console app with dotnet new console, move into the folder, and run dotnet run. Edit Program.cs to make it yours. Remember: C sharp is the language and dot net is the toolbox. Open the whole project folder, finish Module 1, then take the quiz.

title: Tips & tricks for this site
combinedTranscript: Follow Start Here in order. Open Module 1 online before installing tools, pick one course, and use Mark done so your path updates. Read each lesson, then take the module quiz. Continue banners bring you back where you left off, and certificates unlock when every module is complete. Guest progress stays in this browser. A free account can sync when the cloud is up. Keep guest progress as a backup on free hosting. Type the examples instead of only reading them. Break big tasks into tiny checkpoints. When stuck, re-read the tip boxes, then open Help. You are ready. Go Start Here, choose a course, and open Module 1. Watch the Python or C sharp install video when you code locally. Enjoy learning.

title: AI Module 1 — foundations overview
combinedTranscript: This A I course teaches you to use language models like an engineer, not like magic. You do not need a coding install to start Module 1. Focus on clear goals, constraints, and tests. Language models are good at drafting, summarising, and transforming text. They follow structured formats when you specify them, and they speed up iteration when you check the output. They guess patterns; they do not know truth. They can invent facts, called hallucinations. Vague prompts produce vague, brittle results. Use the engineering loop: spec, prompt, evaluate, iterate. Write the goal, inputs, outputs, and failure modes. Keep a small evaluation set and rerun it after every change. Open A I Foundations in the course viewer, copy the beginner starter pack templates, and write a one-page summariser spec with ten evaluation cases.

title: Python Module 2 — variables & input
combinedTranscript: After your first script, Module 2 makes programs interactive and useful. You will store values, ask for input, and calculate. These skills power forms, carts, and calculators. Variables are labeled boxes. Write a name equals a value, for example customer underscore name equals Sarah. Python chooses the type for you, and you can update a variable anytime. Talk to the user with input. Store the answer in a variable, then combine text with f-strings, like hello name. Do useful math. Convert text numbers with float or int, calculate price, tax, or wages, and print clear results with f-strings. Type the examples instead of only reading them. Build the greeting and price calculator exercises, then take the Module 2 quiz when you feel ready.

title: C# Module 2 — variables & input
combinedTranscript: After your first console app, Module 2 adds variables, input, and calculations. C sharp uses clear types like string, int, and double. You will build greeting and calculator programs. Declare variables with a type. For example, string customer name equals Sarah, int quantity equals 3, double price equals 9.99. Choose names that describe the data. Read input with Console.ReadLine, which returns text. Parse numbers with int.Parse or double.Parse, and format output with string interpolation. Calculate real values for tax, totals, and wages with ordinary math operators. Keep units clear in variable names, and print results the user can understand. Follow the Module 2 examples in your project, complete the exercises, check the solutions, and take the Module 2 quiz to lock in the skills.

title: AI Module 2 — prompting basics
combinedTranscript: Move from vague to specific. A good prompt states role, goal, and format. Add constraints like length, tone, and what not to do, and give one short example when helpful. Structure beats clever wording. Use headings for goal, inputs, and output format. Ask for checkable outputs, and prefer clear instructions over buzzwords. Test before you trust. Try good, bad, and ambiguous inputs. Note failures like missing steps or invented facts, tighten the prompt, then retest. Open Prompting Basics in the course viewer. Rewrite one vague request into a structured prompt, and save before and after notes in your starter pack.
